title: Scholar Data - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Tabarrok and Cowen argue the NSF should fund genuine public goods (replication studies and public datasets) that markets underprovide, rather than duplicating status-quo research; Scholar Data's new S-Index aims to reward dataset creation the way the H-Index rewards papers.

insights.claim: Public-goods theory implies the NSF should fund activities that are especially hard to support through university, philanthropic, and private-sector channels, not subsidize research the market would produce anyway.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: A test for judging whether public research funding adds value: does its portfolio differ from what markets already fund?
insights.quote: the National Science Foundation should support activities that are especially hard to support through traditional university, philanthropic, and private-sector sources

insights.claim: Lists of prominent NSF grants look strikingly similar to the 'good' research the status quo already produces, suggesting the NSF is subsidizing at the margin rather than funding genuine public goods.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Challenges the case for status-quo science funding on its own theoretical terms, relevant to public R&D budget debates.
insights.quote: how similar they look to lists of “good” research produced by today’s status quo
insights.locator: But what stands out from lists of prominent NSF grants

insights.claim: Tabarrok and Cowen propose the NSF should instead prioritize replication studies and the production of public datasets as areas markets and universities underfund.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Points to the specific categories reformers would redirect science funding toward.
insights.quote: We suggest replication studies and support for producing public datasets.
insights.locator: If we take public goods theory seriously

insights.claim: Scholar Data, which won NIH's competition to create a data-sharing index, introduces an S-Index that measures a dataset's ease of access, citations, and mentions, analogous to the H-Index for papers.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: A concrete new metric that could shift academic incentives toward producing reusable public datasets.
insights.quote: the S-Index measures a dataset’s ease of access, citations and other mentions

insights.claim: Academic career metrics (citations, h-index, impact factor) count only publications, so data sharing goes unrecognized and is treated as a chore rather than a contribution.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Explains the broken incentive the S-Index is designed to fix; a lens on why reproducibility suffers.
insights.quote: researchers are expected to share data, but get no credit for doing so
